title: Heart Rate
what_it_is: Heart rate is the number of times the heart beats per minute, a basic measure of cardiovascular activity【21†L277-L284】. It indicates how hard the heart is working to pump blood.
spaceflight_effect: In microgravity, fluid shifts and cardiac adaptations alter heart rate. Studies report short-term missions see a ~10–20% increase in resting heart rate【25†L299-L307】, and long missions show about a 20% rise【25†L284-L292】. On return to Earth, reduced blood volume and orthostatic stress cause heart rate to be higher than normal (e.g. ~+21 bpm when standing postflight【26†L410-L418】).
red_flags: Resting heart rate consistently above 100 or below 60 with symptoms
Fainting or severe dizziness with changes in heart rate
Chest pain, shortness of breath, or loss of consciousness【21†L325-L330】
escalate_when: Source does not specify; contact flight surgeon if concerned.
general_actions: Regular aerobic exercise (e.g. treadmill, cycling) aboard ISS to maintain cardiovascular fitness【32†L354-L359】
measurement_notes: Measured in space via wearable sensors (e.g. Bio-Monitor smart shirt with ECG/pulse sensors【30†L49-L56】). The normal adult resting range is about 60–100 beats per minute【21†L277-L284】.
source_title: Microgravity and Cardiovascular Health in Astronauts: A Narrative Review
confidence_reason: Based on a recent peer-reviewed review summarizing multiple astronaut studies.
context_notes: NASA-specific heart rate alert thresholds not found; values above use general medical guidance【21†L325-L330】.

title: Blood Pressure
what_it_is: Blood pressure is the force of blood against the walls of arteries as the heart pumps【34†L31-L34】. It is given as two numbers: systolic (pressure during heartbeat) over diastolic (pressure between beats).
spaceflight_effect: Microgravity alters circulation but resting pressure is often maintained. One bed-rest study reported a ~16.7% rise in systolic pressure【25†L367-L370】, while others (e.g. ISS data) show mean arterial pressure is unchanged in space【26†L441-L444】. Returning astronauts may experience orthostatic hypotension (low standing pressure).
red_flags: Very high blood pressure (e.g. >180/120 mmHg) or very low (<90/60 mmHg)
Symptoms of hypotension (fainting, severe dizziness) or hypertension (severe headache, vision changes)【34†L86-L91】
escalate_when: Source does not specify; contact flight surgeon if concerned.
general_actions: Regular aerobic exercise in flight to maintain vascular tone【32†L354-L359】
Gradual position changes to prevent fainting
measurement_notes: Measured using an arm cuff (as on Earth) or by wearable sensors (e.g. Bio-Monitor measures blood pressure)【30†L49-L56】. Normal adult blood pressure is below about 120/80 mmHg【34†L31-L34】.
confidence_reason: Based on a medical reference (Cleveland Clinic) and spaceflight study references.
context_notes: Astronaut BP responses vary in studies: e.g. +16.7% increase reported【25†L367-L370】 vs. no change【26†L441-L444】. Clinicians should interpret in-flight readings with caution.

title: Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO₂)
what_it_is: Oxygen saturation (SpO₂) is the percentage of hemoglobin in the blood carrying oxygen【38†L25-L30】. It is measured with a pulse oximeter (often at a fingertip) and normally ranges from about 95% to 100% in a healthy person at normal atmospheric pressure【38†L29-L31】.
spaceflight_effect: In a properly oxygenated spacecraft environment, SpO₂ remains near normal【38†L29-L31】. The literature does not report unique microgravity effects on oxygen saturation (not established in sources). Astronauts use controlled cabin oxygen, so SpO₂ typically stays normal unless technical or medical issues arise.
red_flags: SpO₂ consistently below 90%
Sudden drop in SpO₂ or inability to maintain ≥95%
Symptoms of hypoxia (shortness of breath, confusion, rapid heartbeat)
escalate_when: Source does not specify; contact flight surgeon if SpO₂ falls below ~90% or if concerned.
general_actions: Ensure controlled breathing (slow, deep breaths) to maximize oxygen uptake
If available, use supplemental oxygen or rest until SpO₂ recovers
measurement_notes: Measured with a pulse oximeter (finger, ear, or wearable sensor)【30†L49-L56】. Normal range is ~95–100%【38†L29-L31】 at sea-level conditions.
confidence_reason: Based on a recent medical reference (StatPearls) detailing oxygen saturation norms.

title: Body Temperature
what_it_is: Body temperature is the measure of how hot the body's core is. A healthy individual’s core temperature is about 37°C (98.6°F)【48†L28-L31】, typically within ±0.5°C.
spaceflight_effect: Effects of microgravity on normal body temperature are not clearly documented in sources ('not established in sources'). There is no reported standard change in baseline temperature due to spaceflight.
red_flags: Core temperature above ~38.0°C (fever) or below ~35.0°C
Very high fever (39°C or higher) with severe symptoms like confusion or seizures【54†L78-L84】
Hypothermia signs (shivering, confusion) if temperature drops below 35°C
escalate_when: Source does not specify; contact flight surgeon for fever >38.5°C or hypothermia <35°C.
general_actions: Rest, hydration, and light clothing help regulate temperature
For fever, reduce insulation (loosen clothing), apply cool cloths; for hypothermia, re-warm gradually
measurement_notes: Temperature is measured with a thermometer (oral, tympanic, or ingestible), as on Earth. The Bio-Monitor shirt also tracks skin temperature【30†L49-L56】.
confidence_reason: Based on clinical physiology sources (StatPearls); space-specific data are limited.

title: Breathing Rate (Respiratory Rate)
what_it_is: Breathing rate is the number of breaths per minute, measuring how often a person inhales and exhales【58†L99-L102】. It reflects respiratory function and overall metabolic activity.
spaceflight_effect: The effect of microgravity on resting breathing rate is not clearly documented ('not established in sources'). Closed-environment factors (like higher CO₂) could slightly raise respiratory drive, but standard spaceflight keeps respiration within normal limits.
red_flags: Breathing rate consistently above ~20/min (tachypnea) or below ~12/min (bradypnea) at rest
Signs of respiratory distress (severe shortness of breath, cyanosis, confusion)
escalate_when: Source does not specify; contact flight surgeon if concerned about abnormal breathing rate or respiratory distress.
general_actions: Practice slow, deep breathing to maintain lung capacity
Perform regular aerobic exercise in flight to keep respiratory muscles strong
measurement_notes: Measured by counting chest rises or via respiratory sensors. On ISS, wearable monitors (Bio-Monitor) track breathing rate and volume【30†L49-L56】. Normal adult rate ~12–18 breaths/min【58†L99-L102】.
confidence_reason: Based on Cleveland Clinic guidelines and general physiology; space-specific data are scarce.

title: Blood Glucose
what_it_is: Blood glucose is the amount of sugar (glucose) in the blood, used by cells for energy. Normal fasting levels for healthy adults are roughly 70–100 mg/dL【63†L212-L214】.
spaceflight_effect: No direct microgravity effect on glucose is documented in sources. However, appetite changes and dietary differences in space can affect blood sugar regulation.
red_flags: Blood glucose below ~70 mg/dL (hypoglycemia) causing sweating, shakiness, confusion
Blood glucose significantly above ~200 mg/dL with symptoms like confusion or dehydration
escalate_when: Source does not specify; contact flight surgeon if blood glucose is <70 mg/dL or rapidly rising above normal with symptoms.
general_actions: Eat regular small meals with balanced carbohydrates/protein to maintain stable glucose
Monitor diet to avoid excess sugar; consider low-glycemic foods to prevent spikes
measurement_notes: Measured with a blood glucose meter (fingerstick) or lab test. Normal fasting level is <100 mg/dL【63†L212-L214】.
source_title: Normal Range for Fasting Glucose Levels
confidence_reason: Based on standard clinical diabetes guidelines (ADA) via a medical website.

title: Sleep Quality and Duration
what_it_is: Sleep is a period of rest with reduced awareness and activity. Healthy adults typically need about 7–9 hours per night【69†L106-L110】.
spaceflight_effect: Astronauts often sleep less in space: studies report an average of ~6 hours per night on ISS【65†L21-L24】, less than on Earth, due to altered light/dark cues (16 sunrises per day) and demanding schedules. Poor sleep can reduce alertness and performance【65†L21-L24】.
red_flags: Persistent insomnia (difficulty sleeping) or excessive fatigue
Falling asleep unintentionally, repeated night awakenings
Significant performance/attention decline due to lack of sleep【65†L21-L24】
escalate_when: Source does not specify; contact flight surgeon if sleep loss is chronic or impacts safety/alertness.
general_actions: Maintain a regular sleep schedule and dark sleep environment
Use sleep hygiene practices (e.g. avoid caffeine late) and consider melatonin for circadian adjustment【72†L1-L4】
measurement_notes: Sleep in space is tracked with actigraphy (wrist monitors) and sleep logs. There is no strict in-flight 'normal range', but less than ~6–7 hours/night is common during ISS missions【65†L21-L24】.
source_title: Astronaut Sleep Duration Varies by Timing of Scheduled Sleep
confidence_reason: Based on NASA studies of astronaut sleep patterns and NIH sleep guidelines.

title: Mood and Behavioral Health
what_it_is: Mood/behavioral health refers to a person’s emotional and psychological state. It includes feelings (e.g. happiness, anxiety) and behavior patterns. Astronauts self-report mood and undergo regular psychological assessments.
spaceflight_effect: Prolonged isolation, confinement, and separation from Earth can increase risk of anxiety and depression【74†L326-L329】. These stressors may also affect sleep and morale. Communication delays on deep-space missions will create new challenges.
red_flags: Persistent anxiety, panic attacks or depression symptoms
Significant mood swings, social withdrawal, or suicidal thoughts
escalate_when: Source does not specify; contact flight surgeon or medical officer if severe anxiety or depressive symptoms occur.
general_actions: Use countermeasures such as keeping a regular journal and hobbies【74†L338-L346】
Maintain social connections (video calls) and consider therapeutic activities like growing plants【74†L338-L346】
measurement_notes: Evaluated via psychological questionnaires and interviews (no fixed numeric range). Regular mental health check-ins are standard for astronauts.
source_title: Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders
confidence_reason: Based on NASA HRP documentation of astronaut psychological health.
